extracted.intended_audience: aspiring stand-up comedians (especially those trying to break into the New York City club scene)
extracted.subtask_short: getting stage time at Comedy Cellar
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how comedians typically reach the point of performing at elite NYC clubs like the Comedy Cellar — covering practice, auditions, networking, and career habits. Focus is on the NYC open-mic-to-club pathway.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedic talent
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedic talent is an essential ingredient for getting on stage at the Comedy Cellar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article states there are "a few essential ingredients: comedic talent, of course; practice and hard work; and years of cultivating relationships within the New York comedy scene." Talent is presented as the fundamental baseline, alongside the other factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice and frequent open mics
rubrics_metrics.description: Regularly practicing on stage via open mics is how most comics start and improve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a comic tries to attend "at least 20 open mics a week" to get reps; open mics are described as "bombfests" where bombing leads to improvement — "Every time I bomb, I come up with a better joke the next time." The piece emphasizes volume of stage time (multiple shows per night) to 'time it up.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use low-pressure venues for early practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Start in informal, judgement-free back rooms and dive-bar open mics to try material without high stakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freddy’s is described as "the perfect place for a new comic to try out their material judgement-free" — dimly lit back rooms and half-full crowds are normative early settings where bombing is expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing and solitary work
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing at home and developing material offstage is a productive route for some comics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stef Dag notes that "staying home and writing was more productive" for her; the article contrasts this approach with the macho practice-of-many-open-mics approach, indicating multiple valid development strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social media presence and content creation
rubrics_metrics.description: Building an audience and visibility through social media can help a comedian's career.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a comic amassed "more than 100,000 followers on Instagram," aided by hosting a popular dating show; social media success is presented as a complementary path to live-stage experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Launching DIY shows and peer collaborations
rubrics_metrics.description: Creating your own shows with peers functions like amateur clubs and generates stage opportunities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comics often "launch their own shows with peers" to gain performance chances; one comic hopes to launch a DIY night with friends as an alternative route to club bookings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Networking and cultivating relationships in the scene
rubrics_metrics.description: Long-term relationship-building within the NYC comedy community is necessary to access club opportunities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece emphasizes "years of cultivating relationships" and explains that to get auditions or bookings you often need personal connections with bookers or comedians who have been 'passed.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Referrals from comics who have been 'passed'
rubrics_metrics.description: To get an audition at many clubs, you typically need a referral from at least one comedian who has already 'got passed' at that club.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article states: "to get an audition you need to be referred to a club’s booker by at least one comedian who has already 'got passed' at the club." This referral practice is presented as an industry norm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Getting 'passed' (audition success) and what it means
rubrics_metrics.description: "Getting passed" is industry slang for passing an audition and being approved to perform at a club — once passed, a comic can perform there regularly, sometimes for life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article explains getting passed is akin to being initiated at a club; once you're passed you "can perform at the club, sometimes for years, and even for life."

rubrics_metrics.name: Club selectivity and exclusivity (Comedy Cellar is particularly competitive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different clubs vary in exclusivity; the Comedy Cellar is among the most difficult places to get passed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotes: "Some clubs are more exclusive than others, and the Comedy Cellar... is one of the hardest places to get passed at." Ophira Eisenberg calls it "the scariest, most comedians would tell you." This affects strategy and expectations for applicants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audition procedures and sign-ups
rubrics_metrics.description: Clubs may run auditions and post online sign-up forms, though access often still depends on referrals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a comic "signed up online when Rodney’s posted an open audition form," but the piece also stresses that generally you need a referral to secure an audition, indicating multiple administrative paths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage adaptability and crowd work skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Being able to do crowd work and adapt on the fly is a valued performance skill at higher-tier shows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eisenberg demonstrates crowd work — improvising about audience details and doubling down on jokes — illustrating that adaptability and the ability to read and engage the room are distinguishing professional skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polish, confidence, and stage comfort
rubrics_metrics.description: Seasoned professionals display polished material, visible comfort on stage, and resilience when jokes don't land.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Village Underground show contrasted with the open mic: "comedians were noticeably comfortable... Gone were the nervous glances" and the professionals weren't visibly deflated when a joke failed. The article implies this polish is the product of time and repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-term persistence and realistic time horizon
rubrics_metrics.description: Be prepared for a long apprenticeship — significant improvement and career success can take many years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stef Dag: "You’re not going to be good for 10 years." The article frames comedy as requiring an "ego death" and long-term commitment; there are "no short cut[s]."
